vignette: It begins in the dry heat of a border crossing, two decades ago. He is forty-four when the engine stalls. Men in unmarked uniforms step from the shade. There is no warning, only the cold grip of zip ties and the sudden, suffocating certainty that his life is no longer his own. For seventy-two days, he sits on a concrete floor in a windowless room. Time fractures. He learns to breathe shallowly, to fold himself smaller, to watch the door for sounds that might mean relief or punishment. He stops speaking to conserve his voice. When the gate finally opens, the afternoon light feels violent. He walks out into a market he does not recognize, his clothes stiff with sweat and fear, clutching a single plastic bag with his papers. In the years that follow, he builds a life of quiet precision. He marries Priya, who meets his silence with steady hands and warm tea. He takes the job at the distribution center, drawn to the predictable rhythm of forklifts, scanning guns, and high shelves. The warehouse is vast, but he likes the order of it. Yet his body keeps its own ledger. He wakes at 2:45 a.m. without warning, heart hammering against his ribs, hands instinctively pressing into the mattress as if testing for restraints. He stops sleeping on his back. At work, the sudden ring of the safety buzzer sends his shoulders up to his ears. He checks the exit routes during every shift, his eyes tracking the mezzanine walkways and the heavy rolling doors. When coworkers clink coffee mugs too loudly or a pallet jack jerks backward, he flinches, breath catching in a throat that remembers how tight it once felt. He tells himself it is just age, just nerves. He tells himself he is safe. Now he is sixty-four. His knees ache from decades of bending to inspect crates, and his hands bear the pale scars of box cutters and wire. The warehouse has automated since he arrived; the pace is faster, the cameras watch the aisles. He moves through the fluorescent glare like a man walking on glass. Priya notices the way he sets his keys in the same bowl every night, the way he counts the locks before bed. He does not speak of the years in the dark, but they live in his posture: the slight lean forward, the habit of keeping his back to the wall, the way he pauses at any doorway, waiting for someone else to step through first. Some evenings, the smell of diesel from the loading bay drags him backward. For a few breaths, the warehouse dissolves. He is back on the concrete, listening for footsteps, feeling the ghost weight of the door latch on the inside. He blinks. The scanner beeps. His shift supervisor asks about the morning inventory. He nods, swallows the tightness in his chest, and walks toward the loading zone. He drives home through traffic that moves like a slow river. The brake lights blur. His wife calls ahead, her voice bright with the evening plans she has arranged—dinner at her sister’s, a walk along the river afterward. He answers that he will be there, that he is fine. He pulls into the driveway, sits in the car for six minutes, listening to the engine tick cool. He thinks about the door. He thinks about the silence. He thinks about how much work it takes just to stay here, now, in this body, in this life. The house lights warm the driveway. He reaches for the door handle, checks the mirror, and steps inside.
